solutions.check: 28 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: Tending to leak over top of ledge, being ready to drop off

indicators.note: the top of a word written down the grid is its first letter
one piece spreads over another and so encloses it

blocks.note: something that seeps is liable to leak slowly

explanation.surface: A leaky gutter dribbling over the edge of a ledge, its drips about to fall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drop off' looks like water falling from the ledge, but it means nodding off to sleep. SEEPY wraps round L to give SLEEPY.
explanation.definitionFit: To drop off is to fall asleep, so someone drowsy is close to doing it.

clue.text: Dig after broadcaster shows how we can access EU countries

definitions.text: how we can access EU countries

indicators.note: coming after means following, so the piece it governs is placed second

blocks.note: to tunnel is to dig a passage

explanation.surface: A TV channel's investigation digs up the way Britons get to the Continent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' puts the dig second, behind the broadcaster. The Channel Tunnel runs under the English Channel from Kent to France.
explanation.definitionFit: The rail link under the sea between England and France is the main overland route from Britain into mainland Europe.

clue.text: Overturning fast car with one shows your bottle, maybe

indicators.note: overturning upsets things and leaves them jumbled out of their original order

explanation.surface: A car crash is blamed on the driver's drinking, with a bottle found in the wreck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bottle' tempts as courage, as in showing your bottle; here it is a bottle of wine.
explanation.definitionFit: Frascati is a white Italian wine from near Rome, so it is one example of what might fill your bottle.

clue.text: see 22dn.
Britain in a mess, slain, dead?

indicators.note: things in a mess are disordered, so the letters lose their arrangement

blocks.note: D is the standard abbreviation for dead

explanation.surface: A gloomy verdict on the state of the nation: chaotic, murdered and finished.
explanation.walkthrough: Britain is the definition by example; the rest is a jumble of five letters plus the abbreviation for dead.
explanation.definitionFit: Great Britain is a large landmass surrounded by sea, so it is one example of the general word.

clue.text: Available for a price, Noel's touring round the country shortly

indicators.note: something touring moves about from place to place, so the letters are moved around
going round something encircles it, so one piece sits inside another

blocks.note: taken as written, with the S of the possessive
A is the international vehicle code for Austria

explanation.surface: Tickets go on sale as Noel (Gallagher, say) takes his band on a short tour of the country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shortly' asks for an abbreviation of a country; the vehicle code A for Austria sits inside the rearranged name.
explanation.definitionFit: Goods offered to buyers in exchange for money are said to be for sale in shops.

clue.text: see 19dn.
Pro forming union with Ant?

blocks.note: a worker is the commonest kind of ant in a colony

explanation.surface: A professional teams up with Ant, as though partnering a TV presenter double act.
explanation.walkthrough: Ant suggests the TV presenter of Ant and Dec, a British double act; here it is the insect. Pro is short for a prostitute.
explanation.definitionFit: In slang a pro is a prostitute, someone who sells sexual services for money.

clue.text: In gratitude, Brenda reveals privates

indicators.note: one thing placed in another ends up enclosed by it

blocks.note: Brenda is Private Eye's nickname for the late Queen, Elizabeth Regina

explanation.surface: Brenda, overcome with thanks, ends up exposing herself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Privates' looks rude but means private soldiers, and 'reveals' suggests flashing but just links. Brenda is Private Eye's long-running nickname for Queen Elizabeth II.
explanation.definitionFit: Ordinary soldiers below officer level are collectively called the ranks, and a private is the lowest of them.

clue.text: It's forever being discussed, producing ennui – pour one a bubbly!

indicators.note: bubbly liquid is agitated and fizzing, so the letters are churned up

explanation.surface: A topic that never stops being debated is so boring you need a glass of fizz.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bubbly' looks like the champagne poured to relieve the boredom, but it signals the rearrangement of the thirteen letters before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Britain's membership of the European bloc was argued over endlessly in the years around the Brexit referendum.

clue.text: Not much of a declaration by the typical multinational? Result of extra chicanery and deviation

definitions.text: Not much of a declaration by the typical multinational?

indicators.note: chicanery is trickery, so the letters are manipulated into a new order

blocks.note: a turn is a change of direction

explanation.surface: A dig at multinationals whose meagre declarations come from tax dodging and clever accounting.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is that big companies declare very little; 'chicanery' fits the tax-avoidance theme but works on the word before it.
explanation.definitionFit: A tax return is the official statement of income filed with the authorities, which some corporations keep suspiciously small.

clue.text: It was much maligned once, dipping end of prick in drink

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter
dipping something in liquid puts it inside, so one piece is enclosed

explanation.surface: A smutty image of something being dunked in a glass, said to have been widely mocked.
explanation.walkthrough: Skoda, the Czech carmaker, was the butt of countless jokes in Britain in the 1980s before its reputation recovered.
explanation.definitionFit: The Czech car brand was a long-running national joke for poor quality before Volkswagen ownership transformed it.

clue.text: Native Aussie, well on the large side

blocks.note: a roo is a kangaroo, native to Australia

explanation.surface: An Indigenous Australian described as rather well-built.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Native Aussie' suggests a person, but it is the animal; 'well' is the interjection, as in 'well, well!'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something spacious or generously sized is described as comfortably big, with plenty of room inside.

clue.text: United, Hearts, plus journalist, wanker-fashion?

blocks.note: H is the card-suit abbreviation for hearts

explanation.surface: A football pundit sneers at United, Hearts and a journalist as a bunch of wankers.
explanation.walkthrough: United and Hearts look like football clubs (Hearts is an Edinburgh side), but they supply letters. A wanker is British slang for a masturbator, or an idiot.
explanation.definitionFit: Masturbation is typically done with a single hand, so doing something the way a wanker does is using one hand.

clue.text: Date: if taken both ways, an obsession involving Labour?

definitions.note: a phrase meaning laborious; labour is here hard work, not the party

indicators.note: read both ways means forwards and then backwards, so a copy is turned round

blocks.note: D is the abbreviation for date
the word read forwards and then backwards
a cult is an object of obsessive devotion

explanation.surface: A dating dilemma: getting fixated on a Labour figure, whichever way you look at it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Labour' looks like the political party, but it means toil; the little word appears once forwards and once backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A task that demands hard toil and effort is hard, not easy to accomplish.

clue.text: (& 20ac.) Mick in free production, alarmingly on the rise in our cities

definitions.text: alarmingly on the rise in our cities

indicators.note: a production makes something new from raw material, so the letters are refashioned

explanation.surface: Mick (Jagger, perhaps) stars in a free show, amid worrying news about urban violence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like a link inside the phrase, but its letters are part of the ten to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Stabbings and offences with bladed weapons have been a widely reported growing problem in British cities.

clue.text: Elected, being ultimately dense and unfeeling

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter is kept

blocks.note: a party elected is in power

explanation.surface: A jibe that the newly elected politician turns out to be stupid and heartless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Being' reads as a verb but is the noun, as in human being.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone cruel and lacking compassion shows no sympathy for others' suffering.

clue.text: Uncommonly fit, eh? What one does is appropriate

definitions.note: a clause describing a person: one whose activity is appropriating

indicators.note: uncommonly suggests an unusual form, so the letters appear in an unusual order

explanation.surface: Someone is told they are remarkably fit, and that their behaviour is suitably proper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Appropriate' reads as the adjective meaning suitable; read as the verb, to take for oneself, it defines the person.
explanation.definitionFit: To appropriate is to take something without permission, which is exactly a robber's activity.

clue.text: Not standing for drink with Cruz?

blocks.note: the drink is slang for the sea
Ted Cruz is a US senator

explanation.surface: Ted Cruz declines to stand for office, or refuses to rise for a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Standing' suggests running for election, which Cruz did for president; here it is literal, on one's feet.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone sitting down is in a chair rather than upright on their feet.

clue.text: Role: female affectionately working to produce a splendid erection

blocks.note: an actor's part is a role
hen is an affectionate term for a woman, especially in Scotland and northern England
a machine that is on is working

explanation.surface: An actress throws herself into a role in a saucy production.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Erection' plays on its rude sense; here it is simply something built.
explanation.definitionFit: The Parthenon is the great marble temple on the Athens Acropolis, a magnificent structure put up by builders.

clue.text: (& 6dn.) People's Protest: "Break up Tory club protecting incompetent Conservative leaders!"

indicators.note: breaking something smashes it into bits that can be reassembled differently
leaders go at the front, so only first letters are taken
to protect is to shield or surround, so one piece goes inside

blocks.note: the opening letters of the two words

explanation.surface: Protesters demand that a Tory club sheltering inept party bosses be broken up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Break up' reads as one phrase, but only 'Break' is the signal; 'up' belongs among the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: An outcry is a loud expression of anger or objection, and one made by the general population is a popular protest.

clue.text: see 15ac,
Dear, gutless Corby, on the outside of lost movement

indicators.note: without guts means with the insides removed, so only the outer letters survive
movement shifts things about, so the letters are rearranged
being on the outside means surrounding, so one piece wraps another

blocks.note: the first and last letters of Corby

explanation.surface: A letter to cowardly Corby, outside a political movement that has lost its way.
explanation.walkthrough: Corby suggests the Northamptonshire town or Jeremy Corbyn's Labour movement; 'Dear' looks like the opening of a letter but means expensive.
explanation.definitionFit: Something dear costs a lot of money, so it is expensive to buy.

clue.text: A high-ranked Muslim, say, tucked into loaf

indicators.note: something tucked into another is placed inside it

blocks.note: to bum around is to loaf or idle

explanation.surface: A senior Muslim dignitary sits down to some bread.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Loaf' looks like bread but is the verb, to idle about.
explanation.definitionFit: Begum is a title for a Muslim woman of high rank in South Asia, such as a princess or lady.

clue.text: (& 4dn.) Admit defeat, i.e. voting "Out"

blocks.note: surface reading: concede, surrender, stop resisting
setter's reading: casting a Leave vote is cast as yielding to pressure, a jab at Brexit

explanation.walkthrough: A political quip rather than strict wordplay: the setter calls voting Out a capitulation, so the phrase means yield to pressure.
explanation.definitionFit: To yield to someone or something is to stop resisting, conceding that they have won.

clue.text: Sensed tum rumbled ... when driven by Nick?

indicators.note: a rumbling stomach churns, so the letters are churned into a new order

explanation.surface: A hungry belly growls during a drive with someone called Nick.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb is 'needs must when the devil drives', and Old Nick is the devil, so the definition finishes the saying.
explanation.definitionFit: The saying means you do what necessity forces on you, completed by the devil doing the driving.

clue.text: Who makes things up about Niven, the "almost" politician

indicators.note: about can mean around and in disorder, so the letters are scattered
almost means not quite all, so the last letter is dropped

blocks.note: a politician is a Tory, cut short

explanation.surface: A fantasist spins yarns about David Niven and a would-be politician.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks around 'almost' make it look like a description of the politician, but it trims the party member's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who devises new things creates them from imagination, much as an inventor dreams up devices.

clue.text: Salted nuts panned

indicators.note: nuts means crazy, so the letters go wild and rearrange

explanation.surface: A snack of salted nuts gets a scathing review.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Salted nuts' reads as a bar snack; the second word is the signal and 'panned' is a critic's verdict, not a cooking pan.
explanation.definitionFit: To slate a play or book is British slang for criticising it harshly, just as a critic pans it.
